alumni.name: Marcus Johnson
alumni.bio: Attorney, Howard University graduate, and returning mentor to current Beaux.
story: Marcus Johnson walked into his first Academy session as a quiet fifteen-year-old who had never worn a tie. He left the program four years later having debated on a state stage, coordinated a canned-food drive that fed dozens of families, and decided — for the first time with real conviction — what he wanted his life to stand for.

"The Academy didn't just teach me how to tie a bowtie," he says now. "It taught me how to walk into a room I didn't feel ready for and stay anyway." That lesson carried him through Howard University and into Georgetown Law, where the same discipline the program instilled — show up prepared, listen before you speak, represent something larger than yourself — became the foundation of his legal career.

Today Marcus returns to the Academy each fall to run a mock-trial session for the newest class of Beaux. He credits the program's mentors with showing him what was possible before he could fully see it himself, and he's committed to doing the same for the next generation.
alumni.advice: Don't wait until you feel ready. Show up, and let the room teach you the rest.

alumni.name: Dr. Jordan Wells
alumni.bio: Family physician and Morehouse graduate who returned to open a practice in the same community that raised him.
story: Growing up, Jordan Wells rarely saw a doctor who looked like him. During his Academy years, a community-service placement at a local clinic changed the direction of his life — he still remembers the moment a pediatrician there let him sit in on a well-child visit and explained, patiently, what she was doing and why.

"That afternoon planted something," Jordan says. "The Academy is what gave me the confidence to think a kid from my neighborhood could actually become that person." He carried that conviction through Morehouse College and Meharry Medical College, and after his residency, he made a deliberate choice to open his practice back in the community where he grew up.
Jordan now hosts an annual health-and-wellness session for current Beaux, walking them through basic health literacy and answering the same kinds of questions he once had no one to ask.
alumni.advice: Find the moment that plants the seed, then protect it — it will carry you further than you expect.

alumni.name: Malik Anderson
alumni.bio: Software engineer and Georgia Tech graduate building a coding workshop for current Beaux.
story: Malik Anderson was the Beau who fixed the projector before every Academy session — not because anyone asked, but because he couldn't help himself. A mentor noticed, connected him with a summer coding camp, and by the time he graduated high school he'd already built his first app.

"The Academy taught me that being the person who solves the quiet problem in the room is its own kind of leadership," he says. That mindset followed him to Georgia Tech and into a career building software used by thousands of people who will never know his name — which, he'll tell you, is exactly the point.
He's currently developing a beginner coding session he hopes to bring back to the Academy, so the next kid who can't stop fiddling with the equipment has somewhere to point that energy.
alumni.advice: Leadership isn't always the loudest person in the room. Sometimes it's the one who quietly makes things work.

alumni.name: Xavier Brooks
alumni.bio: City councilman and Georgetown graduate from the Academy's earliest classes, now shaping policy in the community that raised him.
story: As a member of one of the Academy's founding classes, Xavier Brooks didn't have many alumni to look up to — he was becoming the example he wished he'd had. The community-service requirement that once felt like an obligation became, over time, the thing he cared about most.

"I learned that leadership is really just a decision to stay accountable to people who are counting on you," Xavier says. After Georgetown, he came home rather than staying away, eventually running for city council on a platform built around the same neighborhoods where his Academy service hours were logged years earlier.

He now sits on the program's advisory committee and makes it a point to attend as many gala ceremonies as his schedule allows, telling every new class that the Academy's real test comes long after the ceremony ends.
alumni.advice: Go home. The place that raised you needs your leadership more than anywhere else will.

alumni.name: Isaiah Reed
alumni.bio: Naval officer and U.S. Naval Academy graduate who credits the Academy's discipline for preparing him for military life.
story: Isaiah Reed says the Academy's expectations around punctuality, bearing, and follow-through gave him a head start most of his Naval Academy classmates didn't have. He was commissioned as an officer in the U.S. Navy after graduation and has since served aboard multiple deployments.
alumni.advice: Discipline in the small things is what makes you trustworthy with the big things.

alumni.name: Devin Price
alumni.bio: Head coach and athletic director who returns each year to lead the Academy's team-building session.
story: A three-sport athlete during his Academy years, Devin Price now leads an athletic program of his own. He returns each spring to run the Academy's team-building session, translating locker-room leadership lessons into language current Beaux immediately understand.
alumni.advice: The team that trusts each other beats the team that's just more talented.

alumni.name: Terrence Coleman
alumni.bio: High school principal and published co-author on youth mentorship, now shaping the next generation of students.
story: Terrence Coleman became a teacher because an Academy mentor once told him the classroom was the fastest way to change a whole community at once. He's now a principal, and he keeps a standing invitation open for his former Academy mentors to speak to his students.
alumni.advice: Find the room where you can help the most people at once, and go stand in it.

alumni.name: Andre Whitfield
alumni.bio: Founder and CEO who launched his company shortly after college, now hiring from the same community that raised him.
story: Andre Whitfield started his first small business while still enrolled in the Academy, using a leadership-session assignment as the spark for what eventually became a full company. He now makes a point of hiring interns from his old neighborhood whenever he can.
alumni.advice: Start before you feel ready — the Academy will not be the last place that asks you to.

alumni.name: Christopher Boyd
alumni.college: Savannah College of Art and Design
alumni.bio: Award-winning photographer who returns to document each year's gala and ceremony.
story: Christopher Boyd picked up a camera during his Academy years to document a community-service project and never put it down. He's now a professional photographer and has returned several times to shoot the Academy's own gala.
alumni.advice: Document the work you're proud of. You'll need the proof of who you were becoming.

alumni.name: Brandon Hayes
alumni.grad_school: North Carolina State University (M.S. Civil Engineering)
alumni.bio: Civil engineer working on infrastructure projects in the communities the Academy serves.
story: Brandon Hayes traces his interest in engineering to a leadership session on community infrastructure. He's now a licensed civil engineer working on public projects, several of them in the same neighborhoods he grew up in.
alumni.advice: The things you build should outlast you. Choose a field where that's true.

alumni.name: Elijah Carter
alumni.bio: Foreign Service officer and Fulbright Scholar who now represents the United States abroad.
story: Elijah Carter says the Academy's public-speaking sessions were the first place he learned to represent something bigger than himself in front of a room. That skill carried him through a Fulbright fellowship abroad and into a career representing the United States overseas.
alumni.advice: Learn to represent something larger than yourself early. You'll be asked to do it your whole career.

alumni.name: Robert Sims
alumni.bio: Municipal court judge and one of the Academy's earliest graduates to reach the bench.
story: Robert Sims was part of the Academy's very first classes, long before the program had an alumni network to speak of. Decades later, he was appointed to the municipal bench — a full-circle moment he shared with the current class at that year's gala.
alumni.advice: Someone has to be the first example. Let it be you.
